title: The ENTIRE History of the Mughal Empire in 10 Minutes
youtube_title: The ENTIRE History of the Mughal Empire in 10 Minutes (1526–1857)
description:
From Babur's cannons at Panipat in 1526 to the exile of the last emperor in 1857, this is the whole story of the Mughal Empire in about ten minutes: an unlucky emperor and his library stairs, Akbar's giant library, a chain of justice with sixty bells, a tiger-hunting empress, the Taj Mahal, the Peacock Throne, the Koh-i-Noor and the rise of the East India Company. Every fact is checked, and uncertain stories are labelled.

Chapters are added automatically.

#history #mughalempire #tajmahal #indianhistory #animatedhistory

beats.say: 1739. A Persian king named Nader Shah has just crushed the Mughal army north of Delhi, in about three hours.
Now he's inside the Mughal emperor's palace in Delhi. And he's shopping.
I'll take the chair.
That's the Peacock Throne! It took seven years to make!
And that big diamond. Thanks.
He carried home so much treasure that, according to the accounts, he cancelled taxes back in Persia for three years.
So how did one family build the richest empire on Earth? And how did they lose it all? Let's go back to the start.

show.text: The ENTIRE History of the Mughal Empire in 10 Minutes

show.title: The Boy King With Famous Ancestors

beats.say: Our story starts in Central Asia, the land of deserts and mountains north of Afghanistan.
In 1494, a boy named Babur became king of Fergana, a small valley in today's Uzbekistan. He was about twelve.
And he had a seriously famous family tree. On his father's side, he came from Timur, a conqueror who built a giant empire from Samarkand.
On his mother's side, he came from Genghis Khan, the founder of the Mongol Empire.
So yes. Conquering is kind of the family business.
Even the name Mughal comes from the Persian word for Mongol.
But young Babur kept losing. He captured the great city of Samarkand three times, and lost it every time.
So in 1504 he grabbed Kabul, in Afghanistan, instead. Then he looked south, at the rich lands of India.
In April 1526, Babur faced the Sultan of Delhi, Ibrahim Lodi, on a flat plain called Panipat.
Lodi's army was much bigger, and it had war elephants. One estimate says about a hundred thousand men against Babur's fifteen thousand.
Boss, they have elephants. Lots of elephants.
That's fine. We have cannons.
Babur tied carts together into a wall, and put cannons and early guns behind it.
The noise panicked the elephants, and Lodi's army fell apart. Lodi himself was killed in the battle.
Babur took Delhi and Agra. The Mughal Empire was born.
Did he love his new home? Not exactly. In his memoir, he complained about Hindustan, his name for northern India.
Hindustan is a country of few charms. There are no good horses, no good dogs, no grapes, musk-melons or first-rate fruits.

show.text: Hindustan is a country of few charms... There are no good horses, no good dogs, no grapes, musk-melons or first-rate fruits.

beats.say: Babur died in 1530. Later, his body was moved to a garden in Kabul, near the mountains and melons he missed.
Babur's son Humayun took over. His name means fortunate. He was not fortunate.
In 1540, an Afghan general named Sher Shah Suri beat him and took the whole empire.
Humayun ran for his life. He ended up in Persia, today's Iran, asking its ruler for help.
I lost my entire empire. Could I maybe borrow an army?
Sure. But I'll want the city of Kandahar.
The Shah gave him thousands of soldiers. Sher Shah died in 1545, and his heirs started fighting each other.
In 1555, fifteen years after losing it all, Humayun marched back into Delhi.
Six months later, he was coming down the steep stone stairs of his library, arms full of books.
He heard the call to prayer and went to kneel, but his foot caught in his robe. He fell, and died a few days later.
The new emperor was Humayun's son, Akbar. He was just thirteen.
Akbar grew up to be the greatest Mughal of all. Over almost fifty years, he conquered most of northern India.
And here's the twist. Akbar probably never learned to read. As a boy, he liked hunting, horses and elephants much more than lessons.
Yet when he died, an inventory counted about twenty-four thousand books in his library, all written by hand.

show.label: Books in Akbar's library when he died, 1605

beats.say: Read me another one.
Your Majesty, that's the fourth book today.
Servants read aloud to him every day, and he had a famously sharp memory.
In 1571, Akbar built a whole new capital city out of red sandstone: Fatehpur Sikri.
There, he built a House of Worship, where scholars of many faiths, Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian and Christian, came to debate big questions.
Akbar sat and listened to all of them. He wanted to understand what each one believed.
Then in 1585 he moved his court away, and the new city was mostly left empty. A common explanation is a lack of water.
In 1605, Akbar's son Jahangir took the throne. His name means world-conqueror.
In his memoir, Jahangir says he hung a long golden chain from Agra Fort, with sixty bells on it.
The idea was that anyone treated unfairly by an official could shake it, and the emperor would hear.
Excuse me! Your official cheated me!
Who keeps ringing my bells?
How often people really used it, we don't know. But it made Jahangir look like a fair judge.
His wife, Nur Jahan, was maybe even more impressive. She had real power at court, and coins were even made with her name on them.
On a hunt in 1617, Jahangir wrote, she shot four tigers with six shots, from the back of an elephant.
Around then, England sent its first official ambassador to the Mughal court.
His name was Sir Thomas Roe, and on Jahangir's birthday he watched the emperor get weighed on a giant scale against gold, silver and jewels.
Is the emperor... being weighed?
Against gold. Happy birthday to me.
Then much of that treasure was given away to the poor and holy men.
Next came Jahangir's son, Shah Jahan. And Shah Jahan really loved buildings.
First he ordered a new throne, covered in gold and gems, with jeweled peacocks on top. It took seven years.
His favorite wife was Mumtaz Mahal. They were married for nineteen years.
In 1631 she died giving birth to their fourteenth child. Shah Jahan was heartbroken.
So he built her a tomb. You might have heard of it. It's called the Taj Mahal.
A French traveler named Tavernier wrote that twenty thousand workers built it.

show.label: Workers on the Taj Mahal
show.sub: the count of French traveler Jean-Baptiste Tavernier

beats.say: The main tomb was done around 1648, and the whole complex took about twenty years.
Shah Jahan also built the Red Fort in Delhi. But all this building cost a fortune, and his sons were watching.
In 1658, his son Aurangzeb beat his brothers in a war for the throne, and locked his father up in Agra Fort.
Can I at least have a room with a view?
Tradition says he spent his last years looking out at the Taj Mahal, until he died in 1666.
Aurangzeb ruled for forty-nine years. He pushed the empire to its biggest size ever, across almost the whole Indian subcontinent.
It ruled somewhere between one hundred and one hundred fifty million people. And it was rich.
The economist Angus Maddison estimated that around 1700, India made about a quarter of everything produced on Earth.

show.label: India's share of the world economy, about 1700
show.sub: Angus Maddison's estimate (others argue it was lower)

beats.say: Its cotton cloth was shipped to Europe, Africa and all over Asia.
But Aurangzeb spent about twenty-five years fighting wars in the south, and they drained the treasury.
When he died in 1707, his sons fought over the throne, and governors everywhere started acting like kings.
That's how Nader Shah, the Persian king from the start, could march all the way to Delhi in 1739.
He took the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond. Its name means Mountain of Light.
After a long journey through other rulers' hands, it ended up in a British crown. Today it's in the Tower of London.
Meanwhile, a new power was rising in India. Not a country, but a company: the British East India Company.
It came to buy cloth and spices. But it also had its own private army.
In 1765, after his side lost a battle to the Company, Emperor Shah Alam the Second gave it the right to collect taxes in Bengal, one of India's richest regions.
Don't worry, Your Majesty. We'll send you a nice yearly payment.
So I'm the emperor... with an allowance?
Bit by bit, the Company took more of India. By the 1800s, the emperor ruled little more than his palace in Delhi.
In 1857, Indian soldiers in the Company's army rebelled. They marched into Delhi and named the old emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, as their leader.

tag.text: Bahadur Shah Zafar, last Mughal emperor

beats.say: Zafar was in his eighties. He was a poet, not a general.
The British crushed the rebellion. They put Zafar on trial and sent him into exile in Rangoon, in Burma. He died there in 1862.
In 1858, the British government took over India from the Company. The Mughal Empire was gone.
Zafar's grave was so forgotten that it was only found again in 1991, by workers digging a drain.
But the Mughals never really left. The Taj Mahal and the Red Fort still stand. And every Independence Day, India's flag is raised at the Red Fort.
From a boy king with famous ancestors to a poet in exile, the Mughals lasted three hundred and thirty-one years.
